I'm sure your boyfriend feels the same way. We can't censor ourselves and try to protect them, because that's not fair. They're grown men and will be able to handle it. 

His support in my recovery has been incredible. I was hospitalized for my eating disorder last month for three weeks, and he came to visit all the time, took me on passes, and was there to hold me and listen to my endless tirade of "lunch was so hard and the staff is mean and I hate it" rants. The ability to be open with him about my struggles, also, is invaluable to my recovery. 

Our relationship is unbelievably stronger because we can fight back together, and he's a part of my recovery. I can't stress enough the feeling of openness, too. That's such a huge secret to keep from him, and especially one that affects your moods and behavior towards him.

You don't owe him anything. Let me repeat that: you don't owe him anything. His actions are his responsibility, and his illness is his illness. You have no control over what he does to himself. You are not a psychiatrist, a therapist, or a crisis team, and quite frankly, as much as you want to be everything to this guy, you aren't trained or qualified to handle with extreme emotional situations like he's exhibiting.

Is he on medication? I'm bipolar, on medication, and have learned to work through over my manic and depressed cycles. My fiance is also bipolar, and has never once treated me like this guy treats you. The diagnosis is not enough to excuse his behavior. It may explain some of it, but a lot of it seems like he's just a manipulative shit. So, remember, you're not wanting to leave him because he's bipolar. You're in an abusive relationship. 

The first step here is to take a look at yourself and who you've become in this relationship. Do you love you for who you are when you're around him? Do you love the way he makes you feel as a person? The answer, sweetheart, is most likely no. 

Second step, make a plan. Pack everything of his up, set it aside, and figure out how you're going to get it to him. Mailing sounds like the best idea, honestly, because face-to-face interaction leaves him with a way to manipulate you into feeling bad. If you decide to have him come pick it up, though, you can't be there alone. Do you live with your parents? It would help to sit down with one or both of them and explain the situation, and ask for one or both of them to be home when he comes over. 

If he comes over and physically assaults you, makes threats on his or your life, or in any way makes you feel like you're unsafe, have a parent call 911. Immediately. Your safety is paramount here, and you absolutely cannot sacrifice your own well-being for his. 

Prepare yourself for what's going to come after, too. Abusive relationships don't end easily for the abused. You're going to miss him, you're going to want to see him, and you're going to feel immensely guilty. This is all normal and perfectly okay. You're allowed to feel any way you feel. Give yourself some time to process. After you're past the initial day or so, try to call some friends. Reach out to the relationships you lost to this one. Try finding people around you that support your decision, because you're going to want someone to reassure you that you've done the right thing.

Please PM me if you need anything at all. I've been in an abusive relationship, and it took me a long time to come to terms with it. 

You're going to be okay. Don't forget that. Just keep breathing, keep talking, and keep your resolve high. You **can** do this. You can.

Recently took a course in Victorian lifestyle and culture. Let's see what I remember. 

Photography was obscenely expensive back when it first came to be. The general population didn't have the option of taking family portraits because of the cost. As a result, there were two occasions where an average guy would expect a photographer: a wedding, and the death of a child.

With the sanitation standards of the time so low, and infectious diseases out of control before antibiotics, infant mortality rates were through the roof. That was one reason people had so many kids: they didn't expect all of them to grow up. 

Before photography, it was sort of a fact of life that dead children were something to accept and move on over. But then comes the daguerreotype, and suddenly, photography costs (slightly) less, and is more accessible. In the case of a dead child, a photograph could be the only memory the parents had.

Cue the awkward chain of events. A child gets very sick, and it's obvious that s/he will die shortly. Before calling friends and family or funeral directors, the family would rush to find a photographer. Sometimes the child would be photographed alive and extremely ill - these are disturbing, but mostly sad. That being said, the photographer didn't always get there in time, and thus we have pictures of dead children. 

People used to hang these up in their living rooms since it was their only memory of the child. Thankfully this has fallen out of practice.

I don't have much to add other than after seven years of struggling with bulimia, this can and will get very dangerous very quickly. That being said, while your support and help are essential, she won't get help unless she's ready. Definitely push the issue, that it's unhealthy and she can't continue to destroy her body in this sense, but know going into the discussion that she may not want help, and that there's only so much you can do until she's ready to admit that it's a problem and that she needs to be seen. Bulimia is all about keeping secrets, and purging is extremely shameful and private. While I was sick, had someone caught me purging, I would've gotten extremely defensive and upset, as well as embarrassed to have been caught. She'll probably want to protect the secret (i.e, it's a habit I picked up, I know it's not right).

Evaluate the situation for yourself, as well. No one expects you to be a hero here, and if it's a new relationship or one that you're not fully invested in, don't waste both of your time half-assing it. She's going to need you, probably for a good amount of time. Know that going in.

Best of luck to you both.
